front_blocks.md: What are the key **features of the endocrine system**?

front_blocks.md: Outline the **sequence of events** leading to an action potential in a taste bud chemoreceptor cell.

back_blocks.md: Chemicals from food bind to the **receptor cell membrane**.
**Sodium ion** channels open, Na<sup>+</sup> enters and the membrane **depolarises** (a generator potential).
If threshold is reached, voltage-gated **calcium ion** channels open and Ca<sup>2+</sup> enters.
Ca<sup>2+</sup> triggers **neurotransmitter** release, which stimulates an **action potential** in the sensory neurone.

Ca<sup>2+</sup> triggers **neurotransmitter** release, which stimulates an **action potential** in the sensory neurone.

front_blocks.md: What triggers **neurotransmitter release** from a taste bud chemoreceptor cell?

front_blocks.md: How is the **resting potential maintained**?

back_blocks.md: The **sodium–potassium pump** actively pumps **3 Na^+^ out** and **2 K^+^ in**.
The membrane is more permeable to **K^+^**, which leaks back out.
This leaves the inside **negative** relative to the outside (about –70 mV).

front_blocks.md: Define **action potential**.

front_blocks.md: Describe the **events during an action potential**.

back_blocks.md: **Depolarisation:** voltage-gated **Na^+^ channels** open, Na<sup>+</sup> floods in, the membrane reverses to about **+30 mV**.
**Repolarisation:** Na<sup>+</sup> channels close and voltage-gated **K^+^ channels** open, so K<sup>+</sup> leaves and the potential falls.
**Restoration:** a brief **hyperpolarisation** occurs, then the **Na^+^/K^+^ pump** re-establishes the resting potential.

**Restoration:** a brief **hyperpolarisation** occurs, then the **Na^+^/K^+^ pump** re-establishes the resting potential.

back_blocks.md: The voltage-gated **sodium ion channels** are closed/inactivated, so the membrane **cannot depolarise** again while the **resting potential** is being restored.

front_blocks.md: Describe the **structure of a cholinergic synapse**.

back_blocks.md: A **presynaptic neurone** containing vesicles of **acetylcholine** and many **mitochondria**.
A **synaptic cleft** between the neurones.
A **postsynaptic membrane** with **acetylcholine receptors** and sodium ion channels.

front_blocks.md: Explain how an impulse is **transmitted across a cholinergic synapse**.

back_blocks.md: An action potential reaches the **presynaptic membrane** and opens voltage-gated **calcium ion channels**, so Ca<sup>2+</sup> enters.
Ca<sup>2+</sup> causes vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release **acetylcholine** by **exocytosis**.
Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds **receptors** on the postsynaptic membrane, opening Na<sup>+</sup> channels.
If **threshold** is reached, a new action potential is generated in the postsynaptic neurone.

Ca<sup>2+</sup> causes vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release **acetylcholine** by **exocytosis**.

Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds **receptors** on the postsynaptic membrane, opening Na<sup>+</sup> channels.

If **threshold** is reached, a new action potential is generated in the postsynaptic neurone.

front_blocks.md: Describe how a nerve impulse **triggers muscle contraction**.

back_blocks.md: Acetylcholine at the **neuromuscular junction** depolarises the **sarcolemma**, generating an action potential.

This stimulates the **sarcoplasmic reticulum** to release **Ca^2+^** into the sarcoplasm, triggering contraction.

front_blocks.md: Define the **sliding filament model**.

back_blocks.md: The **sliding filament model** states that muscle contracts as **actin** filaments slide past **myosin**, shortening the **sarcomere**. The filaments themselves do not shorten.

front_blocks.md: What is the role of **calcium ions** in muscle contraction?

back_blocks.md: **Ca^2+^** binds to **troponin**, changing its shape.
This moves **tropomyosin** away from the **myosin-binding sites** on the actin filament.

front_blocks.md: What are the roles of **troponin and tropomyosin**?

back_blocks.md: At rest, **tropomyosin** blocks the myosin-binding sites on actin, held in place by **troponin**.
When **Ca^2+^** binds to troponin, it moves tropomyosin aside, **exposing** the binding sites.

front_blocks.md: Describe the **cross-bridge cycle**.

back_blocks.md: **Myosin heads** bind to the exposed sites on actin, forming **cross-bridges**.
The **power stroke** pulls the actin towards the centre of the sarcomere; **ADP + P~i~** are released.
**ATP** binds to the myosin head, detaching it; its hydrolysis re-cocks the head, ready to bind again.

cards.front_md: Describe the **cross-bridge cycle**.
cards.back_md:
**Myosin heads** bind to the exposed sites on actin, forming **cross-bridges**.

The **power stroke** pulls the actin towards the centre of the sarcomere; **ADP + P~i~** are released.

**ATP** binds to the myosin head, detaching it; its hydrolysis re-cocks the head, ready to bind again.

front_blocks.md: What are the **roles of ATP** in muscle contraction?

back_blocks.md: It **detaches** the myosin head from actin.
Its **hydrolysis** provides energy to re-cock the myosin head for the next power stroke.
It powers the **pumping of Ca^2+^** back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum during relaxation.

front_blocks.md: How does a muscle **relax**?

back_blocks.md: Nerve impulses stop, so **Ca^2+^** is actively pumped back into the **sarcoplasmic reticulum** (using ATP).
**Tropomyosin** moves back to cover the binding sites, so no more cross-bridges form.
